concepts.def: A species that donates a proton (H⁺) to another species. In HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), HCl is the Brønsted–Lowry acid. A species is classified by what it does in a particular reaction, not by its formula alone.

A species that accepts a proton (H⁺) from another species, using a lone pair of electrons to form a bond to the proton. In NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), NH₃ is the Brønsted–Lowry base and H₂O is the acid. A base need not contain the hydroxide ion: NH₃, CH₃NH₂, O²⁻ and CO₃²⁻ are all bases.

A proton in aqueous solution does not exist on its own; it is bonded to water molecules. It can be represented either as H⁺(aq) or as the oxonium (hydronium) ion H₃O⁺(aq). The two representations are equivalent: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) and HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) describe the same change.

A base that is soluble in water and releases hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq), into solution, for example NaOH(aq), KOH(aq) and NH₃(aq). Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali: copper(II) oxide and magnesium oxide are bases that are insoluble in water, so they are not alkalis.

Two species that differ by exactly one proton (H⁺). The acid of the pair has one more H⁺ than its conjugate base, so its charge is one unit more positive: H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻, NH₄⁺/NH₃, H₃O⁺/H₂O, H₂O/OH⁻. In every Brønsted–Lowry reaction there are two conjugate pairs, one on each side of the equation.

The conjugate base of an acid is the species formed when the acid loses one H⁺ (remove one H and lower the charge by 1: HSO₄⁻ → SO₄²⁻). The conjugate acid of a base is the species formed when the base gains one H⁺ (add one H and raise the charge by 1: CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻).

A species that can act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid or as a Brønsted–Lowry base, depending on what it reacts with. It must contain an H that it can lose as H⁺ and be able to accept H⁺ (a lone pair). Examples: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻. With OH⁻, HCO₃⁻ acts as an acid (HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₂O); with H₃O⁺ it acts as a base (HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O). In any one reaction it plays only one of the two roles.

pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is in mol dm⁻³; equivalently [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. pH has no unit. Because the scale is logarithmic, a change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺] and a change of two units is a hundredfold change. A lower pH means a higher [H⁺]. pH can be below 0 or above 14 for very concentrated solutions.

Universal indicator gives a colour that is compared with a chart to estimate pH, usually to the nearest whole unit. A pH meter (pH probe), calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH, measures pH precisely, typically to 0.01 unit, and does not depend on judging a colour.

concepts.term: Ion product constant of water, Kw
concepts.def: Water ionizes slightly: H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K. Because the product is constant at a given temperature, [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are inversely related: if [OH⁻] increases tenfold, [H⁺] falls tenfold. Every aqueous solution contains both ions.

An aqueous solution is acidic when [H⁺] > [OH⁻], neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], and basic when [H⁺] < [OH⁻]. At 298 K a neutral solution has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ and pH 7.00; the criterion itself is the relative size of [H⁺] and [OH⁻].

An acid or base that is (effectively) completely ionized in aqueous solution. The strong acids to know are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). The group 1 hydroxides (LiOH, NaOH, KOH) are strong bases. For a strong monoprotic acid, [H⁺] equals the concentration of the acid.

An acid or base that is only partially ionized in aqueous solution, so an equilibrium lies well to the left: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq); NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Carboxylic acids, carbonic acid, ammonia and amines are weak. At equal concentration a weak acid has a lower [H⁺] (higher pH) and lower electrical conductivity than a strong acid, but it neutralizes the same amount of base.

Strength describes the extent of ionization of the acid or base; concentration describes the amount of acid or base dissolved per unit volume (mol dm⁻³). The two are independent: 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃ is a dilute solution of a strong acid, and 10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH is a concentrated solution of a weak acid.

An acid–base equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid and weaker base (the weaker conjugates). HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ lies far to the right because H₃O⁺ is a weaker acid than HCl and Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O. The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

The reaction of an acid with a base. Acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water (CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O). Acid + carbonate or hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂; CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂). Acid + ammonia or an amine → salt only (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl; CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl). Weak organic acids such as ethanoic acid undergo all of these reactions.

concepts.term: Salt and its parent acid and base
concepts.def: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the H⁺ of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or an ammonium-type ion. Its parent acid supplies the anion and its parent base supplies the cation: CH₃COONa comes from CH₃COOH and NaOH; NH₄NO₃ from HNO₃ and NH₃; CH₃NH₃Cl from HCl and CH₃NH₂.

concepts.term: pH curve for a strong acid–strong base titration
concepts.def: A plot of pH against volume of titrant added. For 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, the curve intercepts the pH axis at pH 1.0, rises only slowly, then rises almost vertically from about pH 3 to pH 11 around 25.0 cm³, passes through the equivalence point at pH 7, and then levels off, approaching (but not reaching) the pH of the titrant, about 12.5 after 50 cm³.

The point in a titration at which the amounts of acid and base added are in the stoichiometric ratio of the equation, so neither is in excess. For a strong monoprotic acid and a strong base the solution then contains only a neutral salt and water, so the pH at the equivalence point is 7 at 298 K.

pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ. At 298 K, pH + pOH = 14.00, which follows from Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴. For example, a solution of pOH 4.30 has pH 9.70 and [H⁺] = 10⁻⁹·⁷⁰ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³.

concepts.term: Acid dissociation constant, Ka, and pKa
concepts.def: For HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq), Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] at equilibrium (unit mol dm⁻³, usually omitted); pKa = −log₁₀Ka. A larger Ka, and therefore a smaller pKa, means a stronger acid. Ethanoic acid: Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵, pKa = 4.76; methanoic acid: pKa = 3.75, so methanoic acid is the stronger acid.

concepts.term: Base dissociation constant, Kb, and pKb
concepts.def: For B(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ BH⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]; pKb = −log₁₀Kb. A larger Kb, and therefore a smaller pKb, means a stronger base. Ammonia: pKb = 4.75.

For a conjugate acid–base pair HA/A⁻ (or BH⁺/B), multiplying the two expressions gives Ka × Kb = [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw, so at 298 K Ka × Kb = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pKa + pKb = 14.00. NH₄⁺ has pKa 9.25, so NH₃ has pKb 4.75. The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

Because a weak acid is only slightly ionized, [HA]equilibrium ≈ [HA]initial and [H⁺] ≈ [A⁻], so Ka ≈ [H⁺]²/[HA]initial and [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]initial). For 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵): [H⁺] = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, pH = 2.88. The same method with Kb gives [OH⁻] for a weak base.

The reaction of an ion from a salt with water, which changes [H⁺] and so the pH. The conjugate acid of a weak base makes the solution acidic: NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). The conjugate base of a weak acid makes the solution basic: RCOO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ RCOOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq); CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq); HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Ions from strong acids and strong bases (Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, Na⁺, K⁺) do not hydrolyse measurably.

concepts.term: pH curves for strong and weak acid–base combinations
concepts.def: Intercept: a weak acid starts at a higher pH than a strong acid of equal concentration (0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH: pH 2.88; HCl: pH 1.00). Equivalence point: pH 7 for strong acid–strong base; above 7 for weak acid–strong base (about 8.7 for 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH with NaOH); below 7 for strong acid–weak base (about 5.3 for 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NH₃ with HCl); no sharp vertical section for weak acid–weak base. A weak acid or weak base gives a buffer region before the equivalence point.

The point at which half the volume of titrant needed for equivalence has been added. For a weak acid titrated with a strong base, [HA] = [A⁻] there, so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa. For a weak base titrated with a strong acid, [B] = [BH⁺], so pOH = pKb, and pH = pKa of the conjugate acid BH⁺.

A weak acid, HInd, whose undissociated form and conjugate base have different colours: HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq). Adding acid shifts the equilibrium to the left (colour of HInd); adding alkali removes H⁺ and shifts it to the right (colour of Ind⁻). The colour changes over a range of about pKa ± 1, and the end point is at pH ≈ pKa, where [HInd] = [Ind⁻]. Examples: methyl orange, range about 3.1–4.4; phenolphthalein, about 8.3–10.0.
A mixture of several indicators whose colour-change ranges lie at different pH values, so that the mixture shows a different colour across a wide pH range (about 1 to 14).

The point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour. An indicator is appropriate when its colour-change range lies within the steep (near-vertical) section of the pH curve, so that the end point coincides with the equivalence point. For a weak acid–strong base titration (equivalence pH above 7, salt such as CH₃COONa) phenolphthalein is suitable; for a strong acid–weak base titration (equivalence pH below 7, salt such as NH₄Cl) methyl orange is suitable.

A solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. An acidic buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts (CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa), or is made by adding a strong base to an excess of weak acid. A basic buffer contains a weak base and its conjugate acid (NH₃ and NH₄Cl), or is made by adding a strong acid to an excess of weak base.

In CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) with large amounts of both CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻: added H⁺ is removed by CH₃COO⁻ (CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH); added OH⁻ is removed by CH₃COOH (CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O). In an NH₃/NH₄⁺ buffer, NH₃ removes added H⁺ and NH₄⁺ removes added OH⁻. The ratio of the two components changes only slightly, so the pH changes only slightly; it is not held exactly constant.

From Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]: [H⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻], or pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]). The pH depends on the pKa of the acid and the ratio [A⁻]/[HA]; when [HA] = [A⁻], pH = pKa. For a basic buffer, pOH = pKb + log₁₀([BH⁺]/[B]). Diluting a buffer changes both concentrations by the same factor, so the ratio, and to a first approximation the pH, stays the same; dilution does reduce the buffer's capacity to absorb added acid or alkali.

mcqs.q:
Ammonia reacts with water:
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
Which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction?
options: NH₃, as it gains a proton to form NH₄⁺
OH⁻, as it forms when H₂O loses a proton
None, as water is neutral and cannot donate
H₂O, as it donates a proton to NH₃
mcqs.specStatementText: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
mcqs.explain: In the forward reaction H₂O loses H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and NH₃ gains it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor, H₂O, is the Brønsted–Lowry acid; NH₃ is the base.
rationales: Gaining a proton is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. NH₃ accepts H⁺, so it is the base; the acid is H₂O, which donates the proton.
OH⁻ is what is left after the acid has donated its proton: it is the conjugate base of H₂O. The acid is the reactant that loses H⁺, which is H₂O itself.
Water is amphiprotic. Here it donates H⁺ to NH₃, becoming OH⁻, so H₂O is the Brønsted–Lowry acid.
In the forward reaction H₂O loses H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and NH₃ gains it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor, H₂O, is the Brønsted–Lowry acid; NH₃ is the base.

mcqs.q: Copper(II) oxide, CuO, is insoluble in water. It reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate and water. How should copper(II) oxide be classified?
options: As an alkali, as it neutralizes an acid
As a base, but it is not an alkali
As neither, as it contains no OH⁻ ions
As neither, since it is insoluble in water
mcqs.specStatementText: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
mcqs.explain: CuO accepts protons from the acid (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), so it is a base. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to release OH⁻(aq); CuO is insoluble, so it is not an alkali.
rationales: Neutralizing an acid shows that CuO is a base, but 'alkali' means a base that is soluble in water and releases OH⁻(aq). Insoluble CuO is a base but not an alkali.
CuO accepts protons from the acid (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), so it is a base. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to release OH⁻(aq); CuO is insoluble, so it is not an alkali.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH⁻; it must accept protons. The oxide ion in CuO accepts H⁺ to form water, so CuO is a base (though not an alkali).
Proton transfer does not require the base to dissolve in water first. CuO accepts protons from sulfuric acid, so it is a base; its insolubility is only why it is not an alkali.

mcqs.q: Which pair of species is a conjugate acid–base pair?
options: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻
CH₃COOH and NH₃
H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻
HSO₄⁻ and SO₄⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
mcqs.explain: The two species differ by exactly one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. One H fewer and a charge one unit more negative is the signature of a conjugate pair.
rationales: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻ differ by two protons. A conjugate pair differs by one: the conjugate base of H₃PO₄ is H₂PO₄⁻.
CH₃COOH and NH₃ react with each other, but that makes them the acid and base of one reaction, not a conjugate pair. They do not differ by one proton; the pairs are CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃.
The two species differ by exactly one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. One H fewer and a charge one unit more negative is the signature of a conjugate pair.
Losing a proton (H⁺) lowers the charge by one. The conjugate base of HSO₄⁻ is SO₄²⁻; 'SO₄⁻' results from removing a hydrogen atom without changing the charge.

mcqs.q:
Dihydrogenphosphate ions react with ammonia:
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + NH₃(aq) ⇌ HPO₄²⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq)
Which statement describes the role of H₂PO₄⁻ in the forward reaction?
options: It is an acid, as it gives up a proton to NH₃
It is a base, as it loses a proton to NH₃
It is a base, since negative ions only accept H⁺
It is both an acid and a base in this reaction
mcqs.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
mcqs.explain: H₂PO₄⁻ becomes HPO₄²⁻: it loses H⁺, which NH₃ accepts. So in this reaction H₂PO₄⁻ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid. With a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺, the same ion would act as a base.
rationales: H₂PO₄⁻ becomes HPO₄²⁻: it loses H⁺, which NH₃ accepts. So in this reaction H₂PO₄⁻ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid. With a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺, the same ion would act as a base.
Losing a proton is the behaviour of an acid, not a base. H₂PO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to NH₃, so here it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
Some anions contain an ionizable H and can donate it. H₂PO₄⁻ loses H⁺ in this reaction, so it acts as an acid, whatever its charge.
H₂PO₄⁻ is amphiprotic, meaning it can act as either, but in one reaction it plays one role. Here it only loses H⁺ (to NH₃), so it acts as an acid.

mcqs.q: 10.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 1.00 dm³. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
mcqs.explain: Amount of HCl = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0100 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol. In 1.00 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A 100-fold dilution raises the pH by 2 units.
mcqs.working: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol. [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (HCl is fully ionized). pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00.
rationales: 1.00 is the pH of the original 0.100 mol dm⁻³ acid. After a 100-fold dilution [H⁺] is 100 times smaller, so the pH is 2 units higher: 3.00.
Amount of HCl = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0100 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol. In 1.00 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A 100-fold dilution raises the pH by 2 units.
This comes from 0.100 × 10.0 / 1.00 = 1.00 mol dm⁻³, using 10.0 cm³ as if it were 10.0 dm³. Converting gives 0.0100 dm³, [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and pH 3.00.
6.91 is −ln(1.00 × 10⁻³), the natural logarithm. pH uses log₁₀: −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00.

mcqs.q: Which statement about measuring the pH of an aqueous solution is correct?
options: Universal indicator is as precise as a pH meter.
A new pH meter reads accurately before it is calibrated.
A calibrated pH meter can give the pH to about 0.01 unit.
A reading of 7.00 shows a neutral solution at 323 K.
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
mcqs.explain: A pH meter (probe), calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH, gives a numerical reading, typically to 0.01 pH unit. Universal indicator only estimates pH, usually to the nearest whole unit.
rationales: Universal indicator is read by matching a colour to a chart; each colour covers a range of pH and judging colour is subjective. It gives an estimate, typically to the nearest whole unit, not a precise value.
A pH meter must be calibrated with buffers of known pH before use, because the probe's response drifts with age and temperature. Without calibration its precise-looking readings can be inaccurate.
A pH meter (probe), calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH, gives a numerical reading, typically to 0.01 pH unit. Universal indicator only estimates pH, usually to the nearest whole unit.

At 323 K Kw is larger, so a neutral solution has pH below 7 (about 6.6); a reading of 7.00 at 323 K is slightly basic. A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], which corresponds to pH 7.00 only at 298 K.

mcqs.q: At 298 K, solution P has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and solution Q has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K. How does [OH⁻] in P compare with [OH⁻] in Q?
options: It is 100 times larger in P than in Q.
It is the same, as acid has no effect on [OH⁻].
Neither contains OH⁻ ions, as both are acidic.
It is 100 times smaller in P than in Q.
mcqs.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
mcqs.explain: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]. P: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³; Q: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺] of Q, so it has 1/100 of the [OH⁻].
rationales: This assumes [OH⁻] = [H⁺] in every solution. That is true only in a neutral solution. Because [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw is constant, the solution with 100 times more H⁺ has 100 times less OH⁻.
[H⁺] and [OH⁻] are linked by Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]. Adding acid shifts H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ to the left, lowering [OH⁻]: P has 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ and Q 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³.
Every aqueous solution contains both H⁺ and OH⁻. Acidic solutions simply have [H⁺] > [OH⁻]: here [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³ in P and 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ in Q.
[OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]. P: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³; Q: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺] of Q, so it has 1/100 of the [OH⁻].

mcqs.q: A student's data show that an aqueous solution at 323 K has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 2.34 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, so its pH is 6.63. Which statement about this solution is correct?
options: It is neutral, as its [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are equal.
It is acidic, as its pH is lower than 7.00.
It is acidic, as it contains H⁺(aq) ions.
Both acidic and basic: each ion exceeds 1.0 × 10⁻⁷.
mcqs.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
mcqs.explain: A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], at any temperature. pH 7.00 marks neutrality only at 298 K; at 323 K a neutral solution has a lower pH because water is more ionized.
rationales: A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], at any temperature. pH 7.00 marks neutrality only at 298 K; at 323 K a neutral solution has a lower pH because water is more ionized.
pH 7.00 is the neutral point only at 298 K. The test is the relative size of [H⁺] and [OH⁻]; here they are equal, so the solution is neutral even though its pH is 6.63.
Every aqueous solution contains both H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. A solution is acidic only when [H⁺] > [OH⁻]; here they are equal, so it is neutral.

Acidic and basic are judged by comparing [H⁺] with [OH⁻], not by comparing each with its 298 K value. The two are equal here, so the solution is neutral; 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ is the neutral value only at 298 K.

mcqs.q: A solution of nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), has a concentration of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Which statement about this solution is correct?
options: It is a weak acid, as its concentration is low.
It contains mainly HNO₃ molecules with a few ions.
It is a dilute solution of an acid that is fully ionized.
It is neutral, as this much water neutralizes the acid.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
mcqs.explain: HNO₃ is a strong acid, so it is fully ionized at this concentration: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻, and [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. At 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ the solution is dilute. Strength (extent of ionization) and concentration are independent.
rationales: Weak and dilute are different ideas. A low concentration makes the solution dilute; HNO₃ is still a strong acid because it is fully ionized.
That describes a weak acid. HNO₃ is strong: it is effectively completely ionized, so the solution contains H⁺(aq) and NO₃⁻(aq) with essentially no HNO₃ molecules.

HNO₃ is a strong acid, so it is fully ionized at this concentration: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻, and [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. At 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ the solution is dilute. Strength (extent of ionization) and concentration are independent.
Dilution spreads the H⁺ through more water but does not remove it. [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (pH 3), far greater than [OH⁻], so the solution is acidic.

mcqs.q:
Hydrogen chloride reacts with water:
HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
The position of this equilibrium lies so far to the right that the reaction is effectively complete. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: Cl⁻ is the acid, since HCl forms it.
Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCl.
H₂O is the acid, as it gains a proton.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
mcqs.explain: Acid–base equilibria lie on the side of the weaker acid and weaker base. The products, H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻, are favoured, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O (and H₃O⁺ a weaker acid than HCl).
rationales: Cl⁻ is what remains after HCl donates its proton: it is the conjugate base of HCl, not an acid. The acid in the forward reaction is HCl, the reactant that loses H⁺.
Acid–base equilibria lie on the side of the weaker acid and weaker base. The products, H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻, are favoured, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O (and H₃O⁺ a weaker acid than HCl).
An equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid. H₃O⁺ is favoured, so it is the weaker acid; HCl, which gives up its proton almost completely, is the stronger.

Gaining a proton makes H₂O the Brønsted–Lowry base here; HCl donates the proton and is the acid. Because the equilibrium lies to the right, the products are the weaker acid and base, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.

mcqs.q: Separate 25.0 cm³ samples of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) are each titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). Which statement is correct?
options: Both need the same volume of NaOH(aq), as the acid amounts are equal.
The HCl needs more NaOH(aq), as it releases more H⁺ ions in water.
Both acids start at the same pH, as their acid concentrations are equal.
The CH₃COOH starts at the lower pH, as each molecule has four H atoms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
mcqs.explain: Both samples contain 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of a monoprotic acid, so both need 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of NaOH (25.0 cm³). As OH⁻ removes H⁺, the ethanoic acid equilibrium shifts to the right until all the acid has reacted.
rationales: Both samples contain 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of a monoprotic acid, so both need 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of NaOH (25.0 cm³). As OH⁻ removes H⁺, the ethanoic acid equilibrium shifts to the right until all the acid has reacted.
HCl does have the higher [H⁺] at the start, but the amount of base needed depends on the amount of acid. Ethanoic acid keeps ionizing as its H⁺ is removed, so both need 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq).
Only a strong acid has [H⁺] equal to its concentration. HCl is fully ionized (pH 1.0); ethanoic acid is only slightly ionized, so its [H⁺] is lower and its starting pH higher.
Only the H of the –COOH group in ethanoic acid can ionize, and only partly. CH₃COOH is a weak monoprotic acid, so its [H⁺] is lower than that of HCl and its pH is higher.

mcqs.q: Aqueous ethanoic acid is added to solid sodium carbonate until the reaction stops. What are the products of the reaction?
options: sodium ethanoate and water, with no gas
sodium ethanoate, hydrogen and carbon dioxide
none, as weak acids do not react with carbonates
sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
mcqs.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
mcqs.explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate ion accepts two protons, forming H₂O and CO₂.
rationales: 'Acid + base → salt + water' is incomplete for carbonates. CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so carbon dioxide is also produced (the mixture fizzes).
Hydrogen is produced when an acid reacts with a reactive metal, not with a carbonate. The protons are accepted by CO₃²⁻, forming water and carbon dioxide.
Weak acids undergo all the typical acid reactions. As the carbonate removes H⁺, more ethanoic acid ionizes, so the reaction continues until one reactant is used up; vinegar fizzes with carbonates.
Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate ion accepts two protons, forming H₂O and CO₂.

mcqs.q: Methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃Cl, is a salt. Which statement about this salt is correct?
options: It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with water as a second product.
It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with no water produced.
Its parent base is CH₃NH₃OH, since a base must contain OH.
Its parent base is CH₃NH₃⁺, the cation present in the salt.
mcqs.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
mcqs.explain: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The amine accepts a proton on the lone pair of its nitrogen atom, so the only product is the salt. Its parent acid is HCl and its parent base is the amine CH₃NH₂.
rationales: An amine, like ammonia, simply gains H⁺: CH₃NH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃NH₃⁺. No OH⁻ or O²⁻ is involved, so no water forms; the salt is the only product.
CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The amine accepts a proton on the lone pair of its nitrogen atom, so the only product is the salt. Its parent acid is HCl and its parent base is the amine CH₃NH₂.

CH₃NH₃OH, written by analogy with 'NH₄OH', is not the parent base. An amine is a base because the lone pair on its nitrogen atom accepts H⁺, and it contains no OH: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃Cl. The parent base is CH₃NH₂.
CH₃NH₃⁺ is the ion in the salt, formed when the base gained a proton. Removing that proton gives the parent base, CH₃NH₂.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is placed in a flask and 25.0 cm³ of distilled water is added. The mixture is then titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). At what pH does the pH curve intercept the pH axis (0.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added)?
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
rationales: 1.00 is the pH of the undiluted 0.100 mol dm⁻³ acid. The added water doubles the volume, halving [H⁺] to 0.0500 mol dm⁻³, so the pH is 1.30.
3.00 is −ln(0.0500), the natural logarithm. pH uses log₁₀: −log₁₀(0.0500) = 1.30.
2.60 is −log₁₀(2.50 × 10⁻³), using the amount of HCl in mol as if it were a concentration. Dividing by the volume, 0.0500 dm³, gives [H⁺] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ and pH 1.30.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K until 50.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) has been added. Which statement about the pH curve is correct?
options: After 25.0 cm³ the pH stays at 7, as all the acid is neutralized.
The pH rises by an equal amount for each 1.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added.
The curve starts near pH 13, the pH of the NaOH(aq) added.
At 25.0 cm³ the pH is 7, as only NaCl(aq) and water are present.
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) contains the same amount as the HCl, so this is the equivalence point. The solution contains only NaCl and water, and a strong acid–strong base salt gives pH 7 at 298 K.
rationales: Beyond 25.0 cm³ the added NaOH has no acid left to react with, so OH⁻ accumulates and the pH keeps rising, levelling off at about 12.5 by 50.0 cm³.
pH is logarithmic. Early additions remove only a small fraction of the H⁺, so the pH hardly changes; near 25.0 cm³ it jumps from about 3 to about 11 within 1 cm³.
The intercept is the pH of the solution in the flask before any titrant is added: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl, pH 1.0. The curve rises towards, but does not reach, the pH of the NaOH(aq).
25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) contains the same amount as the HCl, so this is the equivalence point. The solution contains only NaCl and water, and a strong acid–strong base salt gives pH 7 at 298 K.

mcqs.q: An aqueous solution at 298 K has [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³. What is the pOH of the solution?
mcqs.specStatementText: The pOH scale describes the [OH⁻] of a solution. pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ
mcqs.explain: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.30. At 298 K pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − 5.30 = 8.70. (Equivalently, [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ and pOH = −log₁₀(2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 8.70.)
rationales: 5.30 is the pH, −log₁₀[H⁺]. The pOH refers to [OH⁻]: pOH = 14.00 − 5.30 = 8.70.
This uses −ln(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 12.21 as the pH and then 14.00 − 12.21 = 1.79. pH is defined with log₁₀, giving pH 5.30 and pOH 8.70.
pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.30. At 298 K pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − 5.30 = 8.70. (Equivalently, [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³ and pOH = −log₁₀(2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 8.70.)
This is 14.00 ÷ 5.30, treating pH × pOH = 14.00. Taking logarithms of Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] gives a sum: pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 8.70.

mcqs.q: At 298 K the pKa of methanoic acid, HCOOH, is 3.75 and the pKa of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is 4.76. Which statement about 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solutions of the two acids is correct?
options: Ethanoic acid is the stronger acid, as its pKa is the larger.
Both are ionized to the same extent, as both are weak acids.
Methanoic acid needs more NaOH(aq) to neutralize the same volume of it.
Methanoic acid is ionized to a greater extent than ethanoic acid.
mcqs.specStatementText: The strengths of weak acids and bases are described by their Ka, Kb, pKa or pKb values.
mcqs.explain: The smaller pKa means the larger Ka (1.8 × 10⁻⁴ against 1.7 × 10⁻⁵), so methanoic acid is the stronger acid and is ionized to a greater extent at the same concentration.
rationales: pKa = −log₁₀Ka, so a larger pKa means a smaller Ka and a weaker acid. Ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) is weaker than methanoic acid (pKa 3.75).
'Weak' covers a wide range of strengths. The pKa values differ by about 1, so methanoic acid has a Ka about ten times larger and is ionized to a greater extent.
Equal volumes of the two 0.10 mol dm⁻³ monoprotic acids contain equal amounts of acid, so they need the same amount of NaOH, whatever their strengths.
The smaller pKa means the larger Ka (1.8 × 10⁻⁴ against 1.7 × 10⁻⁵), so methanoic acid is the stronger acid and is ionized to a greater extent at the same concentration.

mcqs.q: At 298 K the pKa of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, is 9.25 and the pKa of the methylammonium ion, CH₃NH₃⁺, is 10.66. Which statement about the bases NH₃ and CH₃NH₂ is correct?
options: CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base, and its pKb is 1.31.
CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base, since its pKb is 3.34.
NH₃ is the stronger base, since its pKb is 9.25.
NH₃ is the stronger base, as its pKb of 4.75 is larger.
mcqs.specStatementText: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.
mcqs.explain: pKa + pKb = 14.00 for a conjugate pair at 298 K. pKb(CH₃NH₂) = 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34 and pKb(NH₃) = 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75. The smaller pKb means the stronger base, so CH₃NH₂ is stronger.
mcqs.working: pKb = 14.00 − pKa(conjugate acid). NH₃: 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75. CH₃NH₂: 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34. Smaller pKb, larger Kb (10⁻³·³⁴ = 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ against 10⁻⁴·⁷⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), so CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base.
rationales: 1.31 is 14.00 ÷ 10.66, treating pKa × pKb = 14.00. Taking logarithms of Ka × Kb = Kw gives a sum: pKb = 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34.
pKa + pKb = 14.00 for a conjugate pair at 298 K. pKb(CH₃NH₂) = 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34 and pKb(NH₃) = 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75. The smaller pKb means the stronger base, so CH₃NH₂ is stronger.
9.25 is the pKa of NH₄⁺, the conjugate acid. The base has pKb = 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75, and CH₃NH₂ (pKb 3.34) is the stronger base.
The pKb of 4.75 is right, but a larger pKb means a smaller Kb and a weaker base. CH₃NH₂, with pKb 3.34, is the stronger base.

mcqs.q: What is the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH(aq), at 298 K? Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵. Assume that the equilibrium concentration of CH₃COOH equals its initial concentration.
mcqs.specStatementText: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.
rationales: 1.00 is −log₁₀(0.100), which treats ethanoic acid as fully ionized. It is weak, so [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]) = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and the pH is 2.88.
5.76 is −log₁₀(Ka × [HA]), without the square root. Ka × [HA] equals [H⁺]², so [H⁺] = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and pH = 2.88.
4.76 is the pKa. pH = pKa only when [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], as at half-equivalence. In the acid alone [CH₃COO⁻] is far smaller, and pH = 2.88.

mcqs.q: Aqueous solutions of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, and sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, each of concentration 0.10 mol dm⁻³, are prepared at 298 K. pKa(H₂CO₃) = 6.35 and pKa(HCO₃⁻) = 10.33. Which statement is correct?
options: NaHCO₃(aq) has the higher pH, since HCO₃⁻ has the larger pKa (10.33).
NaHCO₃(aq) is acidic, as HCO₃⁻ contains an H⁺ that it can donate.
Na₂CO₃(aq) has the higher pH, as CO₃²⁻ has the smaller pKb (3.67).
Both solutions are at pH 7, as each salt is a product of neutralization.
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
mcqs.explain: CO₃²⁻ is the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻: pKb = 14.00 − 10.33 = 3.67. HCO₃⁻ as a base is the conjugate base of H₂CO₃: pKb = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65. CO₃²⁻ is the much stronger base, so CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ produces more OH⁻.
mcqs.working: pKb(CO₃²⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − 10.33 = 3.67. pKb(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(H₂CO₃) = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65. Smaller pKb, stronger base, higher [OH⁻], higher pH for Na₂CO₃(aq).
rationales: 10.33 is the pKa of HCO₃⁻ acting as an acid; it describes CO₃²⁻ as the base of that pair (pKb 3.67). HCO₃⁻ acting as a base has pKb = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65, so it is the weaker base and NaHCO₃(aq) has the lower pH.
HCO₃⁻ is amphiprotic, but its strength as a base (pKb 7.65) exceeds its strength as an acid (pKa 10.33), so its hydrolysis to OH⁻ dominates and NaHCO₃(aq) is weakly basic.

CO₃²⁻ is the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻: pKb = 14.00 − 10.33 = 3.67. HCO₃⁻ as a base is the conjugate base of H₂CO₃: pKb = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65. CO₃²⁻ is the much stronger base, so CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ produces more OH⁻.
Both anions come from a weak acid and react with water to form OH⁻: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ and HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ + OH⁻. Both solutions are basic.

mcqs.q: Which equation represents the hydrolysis reaction that determines the pH of aqueous ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl(aq)?
options: Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
NH₄Cl(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
NH₄Cl(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄OH(aq) + HCl(aq)
NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
mcqs.explain: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH₃, so it donates H⁺ to water, forming H₃O⁺. This makes NH₄Cl(aq) acidic. Cl⁻, the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, does not hydrolyse measurably.
rationales: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it is an extremely weak base and does not take H⁺ from water to any measurable extent. The hydrolysing ion is NH₄⁺.
This is the salt dissolving. It produces no H₃O⁺ or OH⁻, so it cannot explain the pH. Hydrolysis is the next step: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺.
Hydrolysis is not neutralization in reverse. HCl is strong and does not exist as molecules in water; only the NH₄⁺ ion reacts, donating H⁺ to water: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺.
NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH₃, so it donates H⁺ to water, forming H₃O⁺. This makes NH₄Cl(aq) acidic. Cl⁻, the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, does not hydrolyse measurably.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. What is the pH after 12.5 cm³ of NaOH(aq) has been added?
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: 12.5 cm³ is half the equivalence volume (25.0 cm³). Half of the CH₃COOH has been converted to CH₃COO⁻, so [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa = 4.76.
mcqs.working: n(CH₃COOH) = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol; equivalence at 25.0 cm³ NaOH. After 12.5 cm³: n(NaOH) = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol, leaving 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and forming 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa = 4.76.
rationales: 9.24 is 14.00 − 4.76, the pKb of CH₃COO⁻. At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid it is the pH that equals pKa: pH = 4.76.
8.73 is the pH at the equivalence point (25.0 cm³), where only CH₃COO⁻ remains. At 12.5 cm³, half the acid remains, [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻] and pH = pKa = 4.76.
12.5 cm³ is half the equivalence volume (25.0 cm³). Half of the CH₃COOH has been converted to CH₃COO⁻, so [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa = 4.76.
1.48 treats the remaining 0.0333 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH as fully ionized. It is weak, and with an equal concentration of CH₃COO⁻ present, pH = pKa = 4.76.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solution of a base, B, is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) at 298 K. The pH curve starts at pH 11.1 and falls gently through a region in which the pH is 9.25 at 12.5 cm³. It then falls steeply near 25.0 cm³, through an equivalence point at pH 5.3, and levels off near pH 1.5 by 50.0 cm³. Which statement about B is correct?
options: B is a weak base, and the pKb of B itself is 9.25.
B is a weak base, and the pKa of its conjugate acid is 9.25.
B is a strong base, as the curve has a steep section.
B is a strong base, as the curve starts above pH 11.
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ strong base would start at pH 13.0, and the buffer region and acidic equivalence point (5.3) also show a weak base. At half-equivalence (12.5 cm³) [B] = [BH⁺], so pOH = pKb and pH = pKa(BH⁺) = 9.25. (These data fit ammonia.)
rationales: At half-equivalence it is the pOH that equals pKb. The pH there, 9.25, equals the pKa of the conjugate acid, so pKb = 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75.

A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ strong base would start at pH 13.0, and the buffer region and acidic equivalence point (5.3) also show a weak base. At half-equivalence (12.5 cm³) [B] = [BH⁺], so pOH = pKb and pH = pKa(BH⁺) = 9.25. (These data fit ammonia.)
The steep section appears because the titrant, HCl, is strong. The starting pH of 11.1 (not 13.0), the buffer region and the equivalence point below 7 all show that B is weak.
pH depends on concentration as well as strength. A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ strong base would give pH 13.0; pH 11.1 at this concentration shows that B is only partly ionized, i.e. weak.

mcqs.q:
An indicator, HInd, has pKa = 3.7:
HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq)
HInd is red and Ind⁻ is yellow. What colour does the indicator show in a solution of pH 6.0, and why?
options: Yellow, as Ind⁻ predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Red, as the solution is acidic, with its pH below 7.
Red, as HInd predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Orange, as HInd and Ind⁻ are equal at equilibrium.
mcqs.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
mcqs.explain: At pH 6.0, [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, far below Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁴, so the equilibrium lies to the right: [Ind⁻]/[HInd] = Ka/[H⁺] ≈ 200. The solution shows the colour of Ind⁻, yellow.
rationales: At pH 6.0, [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, far below Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁴, so the equilibrium lies to the right: [Ind⁻]/[HInd] = Ka/[H⁺] ≈ 200. The solution shows the colour of Ind⁻, yellow.
An indicator switches colour at pH ≈ its own pKa (3.7 here), not at 7. At pH 6.0 the solution is acidic, but [H⁺] is too low to keep this indicator in its HInd form, so it is yellow.
Above the pKa, [H⁺] < Ka, so [Ind⁻]/[HInd] = Ka/[H⁺] > 1: Ind⁻ predominates. Raising the pH removes H⁺ and shifts the equilibrium to the right, giving yellow.
Equilibrium means equal rates, not equal amounts. [HInd] = [Ind⁻] only when pH = pKa (3.7). At pH 6.0, Ind⁻ is about 200 times more concentrated, so the colour is yellow.

mcqs.q: Universal indicator shows a different colour at almost every whole-number pH from about 1 to 14. What is the reason for this?
options: It is a single weak acid whose one equilibrium shifts gradually across that range.
It reacts with the acid or alkali present, forming a differently coloured salt.
It is a mixture of indicators whose colour changes occur at different pH values.
It changes colour at the pKa of whichever acid is being tested in the sample.
mcqs.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
mcqs.explain: Each component indicator changes colour over about 2 pH units around its own pKa. Mixing several indicators with different pKa values gives a sequence of colours across the whole range.
rationales: A single indicator has only two coloured forms (HInd and Ind⁻) and changes colour over about pKa ± 1. Covering 1 to 14 needs a mixture of indicators with different pKa values.
An indicator does not neutralize the solution; it is present in tiny amounts. Its colour depends on the position of its own equilibrium HInd ⇌ H⁺ + Ind⁻, which shifts with pH.
Each component indicator changes colour over about 2 pH units around its own pKa. Mixing several indicators with different pKa values gives a sequence of colours across the whole range.
An indicator responds to [H⁺], and its colour change is set by its own pKa, not by the identity of the acid tested. Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators with a spread of pKa values.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three indicators are available, with these pH ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0. Which choice of indicator, with its reason, is correct?
options: Phenolphthalein, as the salt CH₃COONa makes the equivalence pH above 7.
Methyl orange, as its range is close to the pKa of ethanoic acid.
Bromothymol blue, as the equivalence point of a titration is at pH 7.
Any of the three, as the pH passes through every range near equivalence.
mcqs.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
mcqs.explain: At equivalence the flask contains sodium ethanoate; CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes the solution basic (about pH 8.7, with [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³). Phenolphthalein's range, 8.3–10.0, lies within the steep section.
rationales: At equivalence the flask contains sodium ethanoate; CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes the solution basic (about pH 8.7, with [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³). Phenolphthalein's range, 8.3–10.0, lies within the steep section.
The indicator must change colour where the pH curve is steep, near equivalence. pH 4.76 lies in the buffer region, far before equivalence; methyl orange would change colour much too early.

Only strong acid–strong base titrations have equivalence at pH 7. Here the salt, CH₃COONa, is basic, so equivalence is at about pH 8.7. Bromothymol blue's range (6.0–7.6) lies mostly below the steep section, so its colour starts to change more than 1 cm³ before equivalence. Phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) is the appropriate indicator.
With a weak acid the steep section is short, from about pH 7 to 11 here. The pH passes through methyl orange's range (3.1–4.4) in the buffer region, long before equivalence, so the choice matters.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the end point of a titration from its equivalence point?
options: The end point and the equivalence point are the same point by definition, so the two terms can be used interchangeably in any titration.
The equivalence point is the point where the pH equals 7; the end point is the pH at which the colour of the chosen indicator changes.
The end point is where the pH curve levels off after its steep section, which shows that the reaction between the acid and the base has finished.
The end point is where the indicator changes colour; the equivalence point is where acid and base have reacted in the stoichiometric ratio.
mcqs.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
mcqs.explain: The equivalence point is defined by stoichiometry; the end point by an observation. A well-chosen indicator makes the end point coincide closely with the equivalence point.
rationales: They are defined differently: one by the amounts reacted, the other by the indicator's colour change. With an unsuitable indicator they can be several cm³ apart.
The equivalence point is where the amounts are in the stoichiometric ratio, and its pH depends on the salt formed: above 7 for a weak acid–strong base titration, below 7 for strong acid–weak base.
The reaction is complete at the equivalence point, within the steep section. The level region beyond it is excess titrant; an indicator changing colour there would give too large a titre.
The equivalence point is defined by stoichiometry; the end point by an observation. A well-chosen indicator makes the end point coincide closely with the equivalence point.

mcqs.q: Which mixture, made up to 1.00 dm³ with water, is a buffer solution?
options: CH₃COOH (0.30 mol) with NaOH (0.30 mol)
NH₃ (0.30 mol) with HCl (0.15 mol)
HCl (0.15 mol) with NaCl (0.30 mol)
NaCl (0.30 mol) with KNO₃ (0.15 mol)
mcqs.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
mcqs.explain: HCl reacts with half the ammonia: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, leaving 0.15 mol NH₃ and 0.15 mol NH₄⁺. A weak base with its conjugate acid in similar amounts is a basic buffer.
rationales: The amounts are equal, so the reaction CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O uses up all the acid. Only CH₃COO⁻ remains, so there is no weak acid to remove added OH⁻: not a buffer.
HCl reacts with half the ammonia: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, leaving 0.15 mol NH₃ and 0.15 mol NH₄⁺. A weak base with its conjugate acid in similar amounts is a basic buffer.
HCl is a strong acid and Cl⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H⁺. A buffer needs a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid).
These salts give a neutral solution but contain no weak acid or weak base, so nothing removes added H⁺ or OH⁻. A buffer is defined by resisting pH change, not by being at pH 7.

mcqs.q: A buffer solution contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa(aq). A small amount of HCl(aq) is added. Which statement about the buffer's response is correct?
options: CH₃COO⁻ ions react with the added H⁺, forming CH₃COOH.
CH₃COOH molecules react with the added H⁺, removing it.
Na⁺ ions combine with the added Cl⁻, forming NaCl.
The buffer holds [H⁺] fixed, so the pH cannot change at all.
mcqs.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
mcqs.explain: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH removes almost all the added H⁺. The ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] rises only a little, so the pH falls only slightly.
rationales: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH removes almost all the added H⁺. The ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] rises only a little, so the pH falls only slightly.
CH₃COOH is an acid and does not take up H⁺. The base of the pair, CH₃COO⁻, removes added H⁺; CH₃COOH removes added OH⁻.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions; they stay as separate hydrated ions and remove no H⁺. Buffering is done by the conjugate pair CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻.
A buffer reduces a change in pH; it does not prevent it. Converting some CH₃COO⁻ into CH₃COOH changes the ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] slightly, so the pH falls slightly.

mcqs.q: A buffer solution at 298 K contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa. Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of the buffer?
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
mcqs.explain: [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20/0.10 = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 4.46. With more acid than salt, the pH is below the pKa (4.76).
mcqs.working: Ka = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH], so [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × (0.20/0.10) = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(3.48 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.46.
rationales: 5.06 comes from Ka × [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH], the ratio inverted. Rearranging Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] gives [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻] = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, pH 4.46.
4.76 is the pKa, which equals the pH only when [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻]. Here the acid is twice as concentrated, so [H⁺] = 2Ka and pH = 4.76 − 0.30 = 4.46.
[H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20/0.10 = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 4.46. With more acid than salt, the pH is below the pKa (4.76).
0.70 is −log₁₀(0.20), treating the ethanoic acid as fully ionized. It is weak, and in the buffer [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻] = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, pH 4.46.

mcqs.q: A buffer containing 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COO⁻ has pH 4.46. It is diluted with an equal volume of water. To a first approximation, what happens to its pH?
options: It rises by about 0.30, as [H⁺] halves when the volume doubles.
It stays at about 4.46, as the ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] is unchanged.
It rises to pH 7, as the added water neutralizes the acid present.
It falls, as dilution makes a larger fraction of CH₃COOH ionize.
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
mcqs.explain: Both concentrations halve (to 0.10 and 0.050 mol dm⁻³), so the ratio stays 2 : 1 and [H⁺] = Ka × 2 is unchanged: pH 4.46. Dilution does reduce the buffer's capacity.
rationales: That would be true for a strong acid. In a buffer [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻], and dilution changes [HA] and [A⁻] by the same factor, so [H⁺] and the pH stay essentially the same.
Both concentrations halve (to 0.10 and 0.050 mol dm⁻³), so the ratio stays 2 : 1 and [H⁺] = Ka × 2 is unchanged: pH 4.46. Dilution does reduce the buffer's capacity.
Water does not neutralize the acid; both buffer components are still present in the same ratio. The pH stays at about 4.46.
A larger fraction ionized does not mean a higher [H⁺]. In the buffer, [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻], and the ratio is unchanged by dilution, so the pH stays about 4.46.

mcqs.q: Solid magnesium oxide, MgO, is added to dilute nitric acid, HNO₃(aq). Which statement about what happens is correct?
options: MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as NaOH and HCl do too.
No reaction occurs, as MgO is not a base: it has no hydroxide ions.
Hydrogen gas is released, as acids give off H₂ in their reactions.
MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as O²⁻ accepts two H⁺.
mcqs.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
mcqs.explain: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). The oxide ion accepts two H⁺ (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and the salt Mg(NO₃)₂ needs two NO₃⁻ for each Mg²⁺, so 1 mol of MgO reacts with 2 mol of HNO₃.
mcqs.working: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Atoms: Mg 1 = 1; N 2 = 2; O 1 + 6 = 6 + 1; H 2 = 2. O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O, so n(HNO₃) : n(MgO) = 2 : 1.
rationales: NaOH and HCl react 1 : 1 because OH⁻ accepts one proton. O²⁻ accepts two (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O, so the ratio is 1 : 2.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH⁻. The oxide ion accepts protons, forming water, so MgO is a base and neutralizes nitric acid: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.
Hydrogen forms when an acid reacts with a reactive metal. With a metal oxide the protons are accepted by O²⁻, forming water: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O. No gas is produced.
MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). The oxide ion accepts two H⁺ (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and the salt Mg(NO₃)₂ needs two NO₃⁻ for each Mg²⁺, so 1 mol of MgO reacts with 2 mol of HNO₃.

mcqs.q: Solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq). Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺.
NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as carbonates do.
Only NaCl and water form, as neutralization gives salt and water.
Hydrogen gas is released, as acids give H₂ when they react.
mcqs.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
mcqs.explain: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺ and the product breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, which is released as a gas: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
mcqs.working: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Atoms: Na 1 = 1; H 1 + 1 = 2; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2; Cl 1 = 1. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so n(HCl) : n(NaHCO₃) = 1 : 1.
rationales: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺ and the product breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, which is released as a gas: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
The 1 : 2 ratio belongs to the carbonate ion, which accepts two protons (CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂). HCO₃⁻ already carries one H, so it accepts only one: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
'Acid + base → salt + water' is incomplete for hydrogencarbonates. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so carbon dioxide is also produced and the mixture fizzes.
Hydrogen forms when an acid reacts with a reactive metal. Here the proton is accepted by HCO₃⁻, and the gas released is carbon dioxide: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

mcqs.q: Which equation represents the hydrolysis reaction that determines the pH of aqueous sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa(aq)?
options: CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq)
CH₃COONa(s) + aq → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq)
CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
mcqs.explain: CH₃COO⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid CH₃COOH, so it accepts H⁺ from water, releasing OH⁻. This makes CH₃COONa(aq) basic. Na⁺, the cation of the strong base NaOH, does not hydrolyse measurably.
rationales: Hydrolysis is not neutralization in reverse. NaOH is a strong base and does not exist as a molecular product in water, and Na⁺ takes no part; only the CH₃COO⁻ ion reacts: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.
This is the salt dissolving. It produces no H₃O⁺ or OH⁻, so it cannot explain the pH. Hydrolysis is the next step: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.

CH₃COO⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid CH₃COOH, so it accepts H⁺ from water, releasing OH⁻. This makes CH₃COONa(aq) basic. Na⁺, the cation of the strong base NaOH, does not hydrolyse measurably.
This is the ionization of ethanoic acid, which is not what is dissolved. Sodium ethanoate supplies CH₃COO⁻, which accepts H⁺ from water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, making the solution basic.

mcqs.q: Which mixture, made up to 1.00 dm³ with water, is an acidic buffer solution?
options: HNO₃ (0.10 mol) with NaNO₃ (0.20 mol)
CH₃COOH (0.10 mol) with NaOH (0.20 mol)
NH₃ (0.20 mol) with NH₄Cl (0.10 mol)
CH₃COOH (0.20 mol) with KOH (0.10 mol)
mcqs.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
mcqs.explain: KOH converts half the ethanoic acid into its conjugate base: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, leaving 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻. A weak acid with its conjugate base in similar amounts is an acidic buffer (pH = pKa = 4.76).
rationales: HNO₃ is a strong acid, and NO₃⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H⁺. A buffer needs a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid).
NaOH is in excess, so all the ethanoic acid is converted to CH₃COO⁻ and 0.10 mol of OH⁻ remains. With no weak acid left to remove added OH⁻, this is not a buffer.
This is a buffer, but a basic one: it is built on the weak base NH₃ with its conjugate acid. Its pH is 9.25 + log₁₀(0.20/0.10) = 9.55. NH₄Cl being an acidic salt does not make the buffer acidic.

KOH converts half the ethanoic acid into its conjugate base: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, leaving 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻. A weak acid with its conjugate base in similar amounts is an acidic buffer (pH = pKa = 4.76).

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) (pKb = 4.75) at 298 K. Which statement describes the pH curve?
options: It rises almost vertically near 25.0 cm³, from about pH 3 to about pH 11.
It has no near-vertical section near 25.0 cm³, as acid and base are both weak.
It starts near pH 11, as that is the pH of the aqueous ammonia added.
It reaches equivalence well above pH 7, as the acid being titrated is weak.
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: With both partners weak, the pH changes only gradually through the equivalence point (from about 6.1 at 24.0 cm³ to about 7.9 at 26.0 cm³), passing about pH 7 at 25.0 cm³ because CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺ hydrolyse to similar extents.
rationales: A long vertical section from about pH 3 to 11 is typical of strong acid–strong base titrations. With a weak acid and a weak base the pH changes gradually, by less than 2 units between 24.0 and 26.0 cm³.

With both partners weak, the pH changes only gradually through the equivalence point (from about 6.1 at 24.0 cm³ to about 7.9 at 26.0 cm³), passing about pH 7 at 25.0 cm³ because CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺ hydrolyse to similar extents.
The intercept is the pH of the solution in the flask before any titrant is added: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH, pH 2.88. About pH 11 is the pH of the ammonia solution in the burette.

Equivalence is above 7 for a weak acid with a strong base. Here the base is also weak: NH₄⁺ in the salt makes the solution acidic just as CH₃COO⁻ makes it basic, and with pKa 4.76 and pKb 4.75 the equivalence pH is about 7.

mcqs.q: Solution X is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq). Solution Y is 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). Which statement is correct?
options: NH₃ is the stronger base, as solution Y is more concentrated.
NH₃ is not a base, as its formula contains no OH group.
KOH is the stronger base, as it is fully ionized.
Both are strong bases, as both release OH⁻ ions in water.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
mcqs.explain: Strength is the extent of ionization, not concentration. KOH, a group 1 hydroxide, is fully ionized even in this dilute solution; NH₃ reacts only partly with water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left), even at 2.0 mol dm⁻³.
rationales: Concentration and strength are different ideas. Y is more concentrated, but NH₃ is a weak base: fewer than 1 in 100 of its molecules have reacted with water. KOH is fully ionized, so it is the stronger base.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH. The lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ accepts H⁺ from water, forming NH₄⁺ and OH⁻, so NH₃ is a (weak) base.

Strength is the extent of ionization, not concentration. KOH, a group 1 hydroxide, is fully ionized even in this dilute solution; NH₃ reacts only partly with water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left), even at 2.0 mol dm⁻³.
Releasing OH⁻ makes both of them alkalis, not both strong. NH₃ produces OH⁻ only by reacting partly with water, and NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left. Only KOH is fully ionized.

mcqs.q: 10.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of pH 1.70 is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 1.00 dm³ at 298 K. What is [H⁺] in the diluted solution?
options: 0.00020 mol dm⁻³
0.020 mol dm⁻³
0.50 mol dm⁻³
0.0018 mol dm⁻³
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
mcqs.explain: [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ in the original acid. Amount of H⁺ = 0.0200 × 0.0100 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, in 1.00 dm³, so [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (a 100-fold dilution).
mcqs.working: [H⁺] in the original acid = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³. n(H⁺) = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol. [H⁺] after dilution = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³).
rationales: [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ in the original acid. Amount of H⁺ = 0.0200 × 0.0100 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, in 1.00 dm³, so [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (a 100-fold dilution).
0.020 mol dm⁻³ is [H⁺] in the original acid, 10⁻¹·⁷⁰. Diluting 10.0 cm³ to 1.00 dm³ makes the solution 100 times less concentrated: [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.
This uses 10¹·⁷⁰ = 50 mol dm⁻³ for the original acid, dropping the minus sign: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. A solution of pH above 0 has [H⁺] below 1 mol dm⁻³; here 0.020 mol dm⁻³, diluted to 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.
This uses e⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.18, the natural antilogarithm. pH is defined with log₁₀, so [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, diluted 100-fold to 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct equation for HCO₃⁻ acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base in the forward reaction?
options: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂CO₃(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + CH₃COOH(aq)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
mcqs.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
mcqs.explain: HCO₃⁻ gains a proton from H₃O⁺, becoming H₂CO₃: gaining H⁺ is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. Its charge rises by one, from −1 to 0, and the equation balances in atoms and charge.
rationales: Gaining H⁺ raises the charge by one unit, so HCO₃⁻ becomes H₂CO₃, not H₂CO₃⁻. As written, the charge does not balance: 0 on the left, −1 on the right.
Here HCO₃⁻ loses a proton to OH⁻, becoming CO₃²⁻: that is acid behaviour. A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton, as HCO₃⁻ does with H₃O⁺.
In the forward reaction HCO₃⁻ is formed, when H₂CO₃ donates a proton to CH₃COO⁻; it is the conjugate base of H₂CO₃ but is not acting as a base. It accepts a proton only in the reverse reaction.
HCO₃⁻ gains a proton from H₃O⁺, becoming H₂CO₃: gaining H⁺ is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. Its charge rises by one, from −1 to 0, and the equation balances in atoms and charge.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of the conjugate base of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH?
options: CH₃COO
CH₃COO⁻
CH₃COOH₂⁺
CH₂COOH⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
mcqs.explain: The conjugate base is formed when the acid donates one proton, H⁺. Ethanoic acid loses the hydrogen of its –COOH group, so the formula loses one H and the charge falls by one: CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ (the ethanoate ion).
rationales: A proton is H⁺, not a hydrogen atom. Removing H⁺ from a neutral molecule leaves a species with a charge of −1: CH₃COO⁻, not the neutral CH₃COO.

The conjugate base is formed when the acid donates one proton, H⁺. Ethanoic acid loses the hydrogen of its –COOH group, so the formula loses one H and the charge falls by one: CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ (the ethanoate ion).
CH₃COOH₂⁺ is formed when ethanoic acid GAINS a proton, so it is the conjugate acid of CH₃COOH. The conjugate base is the species left after the acid has donated its proton, CH₃COO⁻.
Only the hydrogen of the –COOH group is released as a proton; the C–H hydrogens of the methyl group are not acidic. Losing the O–H proton gives CH₃COO⁻.

mcqs.q: Barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, is a strong base that dissociates completely in water. What is the pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂(aq) at 298 K?
mcqs.specStatementText: The pOH scale describes the [OH⁻] of a solution. pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ
mcqs.explain: Each formula unit gives two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and pOH = 1.00. pH = 14.00 − 1.00 = 13.00.
rationales: This takes [OH⁻] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³, the concentration of the base. Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH⁻ ions per formula unit, so [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, pOH = 1.00 and pH = 13.00.
This divides 14.00 by pOH. The p-values ADD: pH + pOH = 14.00 at 298 K, because taking −log₁₀ of Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] turns the product into a sum. pH = 14.00 − 1.00 = 13.00.
Each formula unit gives two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and pOH = 1.00. pH = 14.00 − 1.00 = 13.00.
This uses the natural logarithm: −ln(0.10) = 2.30. pOH is defined with log₁₀, so pOH = −log₁₀(0.10) = 1.00 and pH = 13.00.

mcqs.q:
The table shows data at 298 K for four weak bases.
W: Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴
X: pKb = 4.75
Y: Kb = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶
Z: pKb = 9.4
Which statement is correct?
options: Z is a stronger base than Y, as pKb(Z) is larger than pKb(Y).
Y is a stronger base than W if Y is the more concentrated.
X and Y are equally strong, as both are weak bases.
W is a stronger base than X, as Kb(W) is larger than Kb(X).
mcqs.specStatementText: The strengths of weak acids and bases are described by their Ka, Kb, pKa or pKb values.
mcqs.explain: Kb(X) = 10⁻⁴·⁷⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, which is smaller than Kb(W) = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴. A larger Kb (smaller pKb: 3.36 for W against 4.75 for X) means the base ionizes to a greater extent, so W is the stronger base.
rationales: pKb = −log₁₀Kb, so a LARGER pKb means a SMALLER Kb and a weaker base. pKb(Y) = 5.80 and pKb(Z) = 9.4, so Z is the weaker of the two.

Strength is the extent of ionization and is fixed by Kb, not by how much base is dissolved. W (Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴) is a stronger base than Y (Kb = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶) at any concentration; a concentrated solution of Y is concentrated, not strong.
Weak bases differ in strength, and Kb or pKb measures it. Kb(X) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ is about ten times Kb(Y) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, so X is the stronger base of the two.
Kb(X) = 10⁻⁴·⁷⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, which is smaller than Kb(W) = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴. A larger Kb (smaller pKb: 3.36 for W against 4.75 for X) means the base ionizes to a greater extent, so W is the stronger base.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is placed in a flask and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is added from a burette. The figure shows four sketched pH curves, A to D. Which curve shows how the pH in the flask changes?
options: Curve C
Curve B
Curve A
Curve D
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: The flask starts with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq), pH 13. Added acid is neutralized while the pH stays high, then at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NaOH)) the pH falls almost vertically through 7, and excess HCl(aq) takes the pH down towards 1.5. Only panel C has this shape.
rationales: The flask starts with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq), pH 13. Added acid is neutralized while the pH stays high, then at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NaOH)) the pH falls almost vertically through 7, and excess HCl(aq) takes the pH down towards 1.5. Only panel C has this shape.

The intercept on the pH axis is the pH of the solution in the FLASK before any titrant is added, not that of the HCl(aq) in the burette. The flask holds NaOH(aq), so the curve must start near pH 13 and fall, as in panel C.

pH is logarithmic, so it does not change in proportion to the volume added. While NaOH is in excess the pH changes little; near 25.0 cm³ one drop changes it by several units, giving the steep section of panel C, not a straight line.
After equivalence the added HCl(aq) is in excess and the solution becomes acidic, so the pH keeps falling below 7 and levels off near 1.5, as in panel C. It does not stay at 7.

Panel B: starts near pH 1, stays low, rises almost vertically about halfway along the axis through pH 7 and levels off near pH 12.5. Panel C: starts near pH 13, stays high, falls almost vertically about halfway along the axis through pH 7 and levels off near pH 1.5. Panel D: starts near pH 13, falls almost vertically about halfway along the axis to pH 7 and then stays horizontal at pH 7.

mcqs.q: The graph shows the pH curve obtained when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is added to 25.0 cm³ of HCl(aq). What is the concentration of the HCl(aq)?
options: 1.25 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³
8.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
1.00 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³
4.44 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: Equivalence is at the middle of the steep section, 20.0 cm³. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl), so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. The intercept at pH 1.1 confirms it: 10⁻¹·¹ ≈ 0.08 mol dm⁻³.
mcqs.working: The equivalence point is at the middle of the near-vertical section, at 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq). n(NaOH) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0200 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, so n(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0250 dm³ = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. Check: the intercept, pH 1.1, gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·¹ = 0.08 mol dm⁻³, consistent with a fully ionized 0.0800 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq).
rationales: This inverts the volume ratio (25.0/20.0). The acid needed the LARGER volume of the two solutions, so it is the less concentrated: 25.0 cm³ of acid contains the same amount as 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, so c(HCl) = 0.100 × 20.0/25.0 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.

Equivalence is at the middle of the steep section, 20.0 cm³. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl), so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. The intercept at pH 1.1 confirms it: 10⁻¹·¹ ≈ 0.08 mol dm⁻³.
Equivalence means equal AMOUNTS (mol), not equal concentrations or volumes. 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq), not 25.0 cm³, neutralizes the acid, so the acid is less concentrated than the base: 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.
This divides 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol by the total volume at equivalence, 45.0 cm³. The acid was all in the 25.0 cm³ placed in the flask, so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.

mcqs.q: The graph shows the pH curve for the titration of 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of a weak monoprotic acid, HA, with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three points on the curve are labelled with their pH. What is the Ka of HA?
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: At half-equivalence (10.0 cm³, half of the 20.0 cm³ equivalence volume) [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa = 4.8 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
mcqs.working: Equivalence is at 20.0 cm³ (steep section). At half-equivalence, 10.0 cm³, half the HA has been converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] = [H⁺]; hence pH = pKa. The curve gives pH 4.8 at 10.0 cm³, so pKa = 4.8 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
rationales: This uses the pH at the equivalence point (8.8, at 20.0 cm³). pH = pKa at HALF-equivalence, 10.0 cm³, where [HA] = [A⁻]; the equivalence pH is set by hydrolysis of A⁻. pKa = 4.8, so Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
This uses the initial pH, 2.9. Before any base is added [HA] ≫ [A⁻], so the pH of the acid alone is not the pKa; pH = pKa only where [HA] = [A⁻], at 10.0 cm³ (pH 4.8). Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
This is e⁻⁴·⁸. pKa is defined with log₁₀, so Ka = 10⁻ᵖᴷᵃ = 10⁻⁴·⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
At half-equivalence (10.0 cm³, half of the 20.0 cm³ equivalence volume) [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa = 4.8 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.

mcqs.q: The figure shows four sketched pH curves, A to D, each for 25.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution titrated with a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution. Which curve shows a weak acid titrated with a strong base?
options: Curve A
Curve C
Curve B
Curve D
mcqs.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
mcqs.explain: A weak acid starts at a moderate pH (about 3, as it is only partly ionized), rises through a buffer region as its conjugate base forms, then jumps steeply at 25.0 cm³ with the equivalence point above 7 (the salt of a weak acid and strong base is basic) and levels off in excess strong base. Panel B has all these features.
rationales: Panel A starts at pH 1.0, which is −log₁₀(0.100): it treats the acid as fully ionized. A weak acid releases only a small fraction of its H⁺, so 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of it starts near pH 3, and its equivalence point lies above 7, as in panel B. Panel A, starting at pH 1 with equivalence at 7, is a strong acid with a strong base.

The steep section is produced by the STRONG titrant: near equivalence a single drop of NaOH switches the flask from slight excess acid to slight excess strong base. A weak acid with a strong base therefore still has a near-vertical section (panel B). A curve with no steep section, panel C, is a weak acid with a weak base.

A weak acid starts at a moderate pH (about 3, as it is only partly ionized), rises through a buffer region as its conjugate base forms, then jumps steeply at 25.0 cm³ with the equivalence point above 7 (the salt of a weak acid and strong base is basic) and levels off in excess strong base. Panel B has all these features.

The intercept on the pH axis is the pH of the solution in the flask, not of the NaOH in the burette. A curve starting at pH 13 and falling (panel D) is a strong base being titrated with acid. A weak acid in the flask starts near pH 3 and rises, as in panel B.

Panel A: starts near pH 1, rises almost vertically about halfway along the axis through pH 7, levels near 12.5. Panel B: starts near pH 3, rises gently through a shallow region, then steeply about halfway along the axis from about pH 7 to 11, levels near 12.5. Panel C: starts near pH 3, rises gently with no vertical section, passing pH 7 about halfway along the axis, ends near 9. Panel D: starts near pH 13, falls steeply about halfway along the axis through pH 7, levels near 1.5.

mcqs.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of a weak acid, HA (pKa = 4.8), is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. The graph shows the pH curve, with the colour-change range of methyl red shaded. Which statement about using methyl red as the indicator for this titration is correct?
options: It is unsuitable, as it changes colour gradually in the buffer region, before the equivalence point.
It is suitable, as its range includes the pKa of HA, where the indicator should change.
It is suitable, as the pH of the flask passes through its range during the titration.
It is unsuitable, as its range does not include pH 7, the pH at the equivalence point.
mcqs.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
mcqs.explain: The curve crosses the shaded band (pH 4.4–6.2) between about 7 cm³ and 24 cm³, in the gently sloping buffer region, so the colour changes gradually and is complete before the steep section at 25.0 cm³. An indicator must change within the steep section, where the equivalence pH (about 8.7) lies, for example phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0).
rationales: The curve crosses the shaded band (pH 4.4–6.2) between about 7 cm³ and 24 cm³, in the gently sloping buffer region, so the colour changes gradually and is complete before the steep section at 25.0 cm³. An indicator must change within the steep section, where the equivalence pH (about 8.7) lies, for example phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0).

The end point should match the pH at EQUIVALENCE, not the pKa of the acid being titrated. pH 4.8 is reached at half-equivalence, 12.5 cm³, far before the steep section; an indicator changing there would give a titre about half the true value.

The pH passes through 4.4–6.2 in the buffer region, between about 7 and 24 cm³, not in the steep section at 25.0 cm³. The colour change must coincide with the equivalence point, so only an indicator whose range lies within the steep section (about pH 7–11) is suitable.

The equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is above 7 (about 8.7 here, read from the middle of the steep section), because the ethanoate-like anion A⁻ is a base. Methyl red is unsuitable because its range lies in the buffer region, not because it misses pH 7.
