mcqs.q: The graph shows the pH curve for 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) at 298 K. pKa(NH₄⁺) = 9.25. The four bars beside the curve show the colour-change ranges of four indicators, 1 to 4, on the same pH scale. Which indicator is suitable for this titration?
options: Indicator 4
Indicator 2
Indicator 3
Indicator 1
mcqs.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
mcqs.explain: The equivalence point is at the middle of the steep section at 25.0 cm³, about pH 5.3 (the salt NH₄Cl is acidic, as NH₄⁺ is a weak acid). Indicator 2 (pH 4.4–6.2) is the only range that lies within the steep section and includes the equivalence pH, so its end point coincides with the equivalence point.
mcqs.working: Equivalence is at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NH₃) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol). The flask then contains NH₄Cl(aq), [NH₄⁺] = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0500 dm³ = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³; Ka(NH₄⁺) = 10⁻⁹·²⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, so [H⁺] = √(5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0500) = 5.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ and pH ≈ 5.3, read from the middle of the steep section. The steep section spans roughly pH 3.5–7. Only bar 2 (4.4–6.2) lies within it and includes 5.3.
rationales: Bar 4 (8.3–10.0) includes 9.25, the pKa of NH₄⁺ given in the stem, which is the pH at half-equivalence (12.5 cm³). But the indicator must change at the EQUIVALENCE pH, about 5.3. Indicator 4 would change colour in the buffer region, about halfway through the titration.

The equivalence point is at the middle of the steep section at 25.0 cm³, about pH 5.3 (the salt NH₄Cl is acidic, as NH₄⁺ is a weak acid). Indicator 2 (pH 4.4–6.2) is the only range that lies within the steep section and includes the equivalence pH, so its end point coincides with the equivalence point.

Equivalence is at pH 7 only for a strong acid with a strong base. Here the salt is NH₄Cl, whose cation NH₄⁺ is a weak acid, so the equivalence pH is about 5.3. Bar 3 (6.8–8.4) lies above the steep section and would change colour before equivalence.

Bar 1 (1.2–2.8) matches the flat region after the steep section, but that region is excess HCl(aq), well past equivalence. The end point must lie in the steep section around 25.0 cm³, where the pH is about 5.3, so indicator 2 is required.

mcqs.q: The chart shows the concentrations of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻ in four buffer solutions, P to S, all at 298 K. Which buffer has the lowest pH?
options: Buffer Q
Buffer R
Buffer P
Buffer S
mcqs.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
mcqs.explain: [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻], so the lowest pH belongs to the largest acid : base ratio. P has 0.20/0.10 = 2; Q and S have a ratio of 1 (pH = pKa) and R has 0.10/0.30 = 0.33. P has the largest ratio and so the lowest pH (about 4.5).
rationales: Q contains the most ethanoic acid, but it contains equally much ethanoate, so [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1 and pH = pKa (4.76). The pH depends on the ratio, not on the amount of acid alone; P's ratio of 2 gives a lower pH.

R has the largest [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] ratio (3), but [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻], with the ACID on top. A large proportion of conjugate base makes [H⁺] small, so R has the highest pH (about 5.2), not the lowest.

[H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻], so the lowest pH belongs to the largest acid : base ratio. P has 0.20/0.10 = 2; Q and S have a ratio of 1 (pH = pKa) and R has 0.10/0.30 = 0.33. P has the largest ratio and so the lowest pH (about 4.5).

S is the most dilute buffer, but [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] depends only on the ratio, which is 1 for S. Its pH equals pKa (4.76), the same as Q; dilution does not lower a buffer's pH. P, with a ratio of 2, has the lowest pH.

mcqs.q: At 298 K, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solutions have these pH values: HCl 1.0; CH₃COOH 2.9; NH₃ 11.1; NaOH 13.0. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: HCl is only partly ionized in solution, as its pH is 1.0 rather than 0.0.
NH₃ is a strong base, as its solution has a pH well above 7, at 11.1.
NH₃(aq) needs less HCl(aq) than an equal volume of NaOH(aq) does.
CH₃COOH is a weak acid, as its [H⁺] is far below 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
mcqs.explain: pH 2.9 means [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, only about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acid. Most of the CH₃COOH is un-ionized, which is what 'weak' means. HCl at the same concentration gives pH 1.0, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³: complete ionization.
mcqs.working: HCl: pH 1.0 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁰ = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, equal to the acid concentration (complete ionization). CH₃COOH: pH 2.9 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial ionization). NaOH: pH 13.0 gives [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (complete). NH₃: pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹², [OH⁻] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial).
rationales: pH 1.0 corresponds to [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, exactly the concentration of the acid, so every HCl molecule has ionized. pH 0.0 would need [H⁺] = 1.0 mol dm⁻³, ten times more than is present.

An alkaline pH shows only that OH⁻ is present. pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ammonia; the strong base NaOH at the same concentration reaches pH 13.0. NH₃ is a weak base.

Equal volumes of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) and NaOH(aq) contain equal amounts of base and need equal amounts of HCl. As the acid reacts, the NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ equilibrium shifts right until all the ammonia has reacted; these pH data say nothing about the titre.

pH 2.9 means [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, only about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acid. Most of the CH₃COOH is un-ionized, which is what 'weak' means. HCl at the same concentration gives pH 1.0, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³: complete ionization.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Chemistry (guide first assessment 2025); topic R3.1 Proton transfer reactions

specStatements.text: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce the Brønsted–Lowry acid and base in a reaction. A proton in aqueous solution can be represented as both H⁺(aq) and H₃O⁺(aq). The distinction between the terms “base” and “alkali” should be understood.

specStatements.text: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce the formula of the conjugate acid or base of any Brønsted–Lowry base or acid.

specStatements.text: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
specStatements.guidance: Interpret and formulate equations to show acid–base reactions of these species.

specStatements.text: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
specStatements.guidance: Perform calculations involving the logarithmic relationship between pH and [H⁺]. Include the estimation of pH using universal indicator, and the precise measurement of pH using a pH meter/probe. The equations for pH are given in the data booklet.

specStatements.text: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
specStatements.guidance: Recognize solutions as acidic, neutral and basic from the relative values of [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. The equation for Kw and its value at 298 K are given in the data booklet.

specStatements.text: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
specStatements.guidance: Recognize that acid–base equilibria lie in the direction of the weaker conjugate. HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ are strong acids, and group 1 hydroxides are strong bases. The distinction between strong and weak acids or bases and concentrated and dilute reagents should be covered.

specStatements.text: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
specStatements.guidance: Formulate equations for the reactions between acids and metal oxides, metal hydroxides, hydrogencarbonates and carbonates. Identify the parent acid and base of different salts. Bases should include ammonia, amines, soluble carbonates and hydrogencarbonates; acids should include organic acids.

specStatements.text: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
specStatements.guidance: Sketch and interpret the general shape of the pH curve. Interpretation should include the intercept with the pH axis and equivalence point. Only monoprotic neutralization reactions will be assessed.

specStatements.text: The pOH scale describes the [OH⁻] of a solution. pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ
specStatements.guidance: Interconvert [H⁺], [OH⁻], pH and pOH values. The equations for pOH are given in the data booklet.

specStatements.text: The strengths of weak acids and bases are described by their Ka, Kb, pKa or pKb values.
specStatements.guidance: Interpret the relative strengths of acids and bases from these data.

specStatements.text: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.
specStatements.guidance: Solve problems involving these values. The use of quadratic equations is not expected in calculations.

specStatements.text: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
specStatements.guidance: Construct equations for the hydrolysis of ions in a salt, and predict the effect of each ion on the pH of the salt solution. Examples should include the ammonium ion NH₄⁺, the carboxylate ion RCOO⁻, the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻, and the hydrogencarbonate ion HCO₃⁻. The acidity of hydrated transition element ions and Al³⁺(aq) is not required.

specStatements.text: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
specStatements.guidance: Interpret the general shapes of pH curves for all four combinations of strong and weak acids and bases. Interpretation should include: intercept with the pH axis, equivalence point, buffer region, points where pH = pKa or pOH = pKb.

specStatements.text: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
specStatements.guidance: Construct equilibria expressions to show why the colour of an indicator changes with pH. The generalized formula HInd(aq) can be used to represent the undissociated form of an indicator. Examples of indicators with their pH range are given in the data booklet. Include universal indicator as a mixture of many indicators with a wide pH range of colour change.

specStatements.text: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
specStatements.guidance: Identify an appropriate indicator for a titration from the identity of the salt and the pH range of the indicator. Distinguish between the terms “end point” and “equivalence point”.

specStatements.text: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
specStatements.guidance: Describe the composition of acidic and basic buffers and explain their actions.

specStatements.text: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
specStatements.guidance: Solve problems involving the composition and pH of a buffer solution, using the equilibrium constant. Include explanation of the effect of dilution of a buffer.
